strengths: Introduces NAS-Bench-Tabular, a genuinely useful community resource: 160,000 fully trained MLP architectures across three real-world tabular datasets (Frappe, Diabetes, Criteo) with training/evaluation statistics, addressing the acknowledged lack of NAS benchmarks for tabular data. Statistics (ECDFs, parameter-count vs. AUC analysis) are reported and consistent with prior work.

Systematic benchmarking of nine existing zero-cost proxies on tabular data, which had not previously been studied in this domain, with SRCC measurements, computational cost analysis, and transferability tests on image benchmarks (Table 15).

ExpressFlow is well-motivated and thoroughly analyzed: ablations on parameter positivity (up to 78.8% correlation improvement on Criteo), initialization, batch size, and recalibration weights (Tables 4-8), plus theoretical analysis connecting neuron saliency to synaptic saliency (Appendix G.3).

The two-phase filtering/refinement design with a budget-aware coordinator directly targets the anytime NAS problem, and the paper honestly reports where the filtering phase alone fails (Figure 5), motivating the refinement phase.

Strong empirical results with appropriate statistical treatment (100 runs, median values, error bands in Figures 4 and 6), and comparisons against a broad set of baselines: search strategies (RS/RL/RE/BOHB), warmup and move-proposal hybrid strategies (Table 11), and one-shot/weight-sharing NAS (Table 12).

Good reproducibility practices: code and data released (Appendix I), pseudocode for both phases, the NAS best-practices checklist is explicitly addressed, and hyperparameter configurations are documented.
weaknesses: The search space is very restrictive: only layer widths of a 4-layer MLP (no skip connections, feature interaction layers, attention, embeddings choices, etc.). Claims of 'NAS on tabular data' and the generality of the anytime framework are therefore limited; it is unclear ExpressFlow and the coordinator would work for richer tabular architectures.

ExpressFlow's novelty over SynFlow is modest. The theoretical analysis (Appendix G.3) itself shows neuron saliency reduces to a sum of SynFlow-style synaptic saliency terms, and in the data-agnostic mode (all-ones input, Appendix G.4) it becomes essentially SynFlow with neuron-wise aggregation and heuristic depth/width recalibration. SRCC gains over SynFlow are small on two of three datasets (0.82 vs 0.77 on Frappe, 0.73 vs 0.68 on Diabetes).

The 'budget-aware coordinator' is oversold: Equation 2 is not actually optimized; the key constants (M/K ≈ 30, U = 2) are chosen from empirical sensitivity analysis (Appendix E), making the coordinator a heuristic scheduling rule rather than a principled joint optimization.

Evaluation is confined to the authors' own benchmark and its three binary-classification datasets; no regression, multiclass, or additional tabular tasks are tested, and the anytime comparison baselines (RE-NAS, TabNAS) were not designed for anytime operation, which somewhat favors ATLAS in Figure 6.

The theory connecting ExpressFlow to 'expressivity' via trajectory length is heuristic; the recalibration weight K_l/l(z^l) is justified by analogy rather than derivation, and the expressivity characterization is asserted more than proven.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('refinemnet', 'Empirically analysis'), Figure 2 axes labeled 'Accuracy' while the text refers to AUC, and some notation (trajectory length z^l(t)) is only loosely defined in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: no existing work supports anytime NAS on tabular data, and the proposed two-phase (filtering + refinement) design with a budget-aware coordinator is a sensible mechanism to deliver architecture quality monotonically with increasing time budget.

The construction of NAS-Bench-Tabular (160,000 fully trained MLP architectures across Frappe, Diabetes, and Criteo with training/validation statistics) is a useful community resource and follows recognized NAS benchmarking best practices (Appendix B checklist).
Empirical evaluation of nine existing zero-cost proxies on tabular data (Table 1, Tables 13-15) is a valuable contribution in itself, and includes transferability checks on image benchmarks.

The paper includes extensive ablations (initialization, batch size, parameter positivity, recalibration weights, M/K and U sensitivity, noise injection) and provides code, data, and reproduction instructions (Appendix I), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The search space is very narrow: a 4-layer MLP where only hidden layer widths vary (|H|=20, so only 20^4 = 160,000 encodings). Modern tabular NAS work (e.g., AgEBO-Tabular) considers richer spaces including operators and hyperparameters; the claimed comprehensiveness of the benchmark is overstated, which weakens the significance of both the benchmark and the ATLAS results.

Novelty of ExpressFlow is limited. The paper's own theoretical analysis (Appendix G.3, Eq. 10) shows neuron saliency reduces to the absolute value of summed SynFlow-style synaptic saliency of outgoing parameters, i.e., a neuron-wise SynFlow variant with depth/width recalibration. The SRCC gains over SynFlow and NASWOT (e.g., 0.82 vs 0.77 on Frappe) are modest, and the absolute correlations (0.73-0.90) are far from a reliable ranking signal, which the paper itself acknowledges by needing a refinement phase.

The core 'budget-aware coordinator' is largely a heuristic: the key design constants (M/K ≈ 30, U = 2) are selected empirically from the same datasets used for evaluation, raising concerns about overfitting the coordinator to the benchmarks. The optimization 'objective' in Eq. 2 has no principled formulation beyond a time-feasibility constraint.

Figure 5 shows that more search budget with ExpressFlow can yield higher-scored but lower-AUC architectures, which undermines the central claim that ExpressFlow effectively tracks architecture performance; the paper downplays this inconsistency.

Experimental comparison to prior art is thin: the main anytime comparison (Section 4.3) is only against RE-NAS and TabNAS, both training-based. Stronger or more recent tabular AutoML/NAS baselines are relegated to appendix or omitted, and all evaluation is on only three datasets, two of which are small.

The anytime NAS framing and the two-phase training-free/training-based combination follow existing ideas (zero-cost proxies from Abdel fattah et al. 2021; successive halving from Jamieson & Talwalkar 2016); the组装 is reasonable but incremental.

The 'theoretical analysis' is mostly algebraic rewriting showing ExpressFlow relates to SynFlow-type saliency; claims that it characterizes 'expressivity' are not substantiated by any formal result connecting the recalibration weight 1/l(z^l) to representational capacity.

Hyperparameter tuning for the benchmark (epochs, learning rate, batch size) is chosen per dataset via grid search on a few architectures, which may disadvantage some regions of the search space and confound the reported AUCs.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: anytime NAS (returning good architectures under any time budget) has not been studied for tabular data, and the motivation is practical for cost-sensitive cloud/industry settings.

The construction of NAS-Bench-Tabular (160,000 architectures over three real-world datasets with training/evaluation statistics) is a useful community resource that enables benchmarking future NAS methods on tabular data, following best practices from NAS-Bench-101/201.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: benchmarking of nine existing zero-cost proxies on tabular data (Table 1), sensitivity/ablation studies (batch size, initialization, recalibration weights, K/U/M trade-offs, noise injection in the refinement phase, Table 9), comparisons with additional baselines including warmup/move-proposal combinations and one-shot NAS (Appendix F), and transferability checks on image benchmarks (Table 15).

ATLAS consistently outperforms RE-NAS and TabNAS in the anytime setting across all time budgets (Figure 6), including very small budgets (seconds) where baselines fail because a single architecture evaluation takes minutes; this is a clear, well-demonstrated capability.

Reproducibility is strong: code and benchmark data are released, training hyperparameters are specified, error bands over 100 runs are reported, and the NAS research checklist is explicitly addressed (Appendix B).

The derivation in Appendix G.3 clarifies that ExpressFlow relates neuron saliency to aggregated SynFlow-style synaptic saliency, giving the proxy some conceptual grounding and honestly situating it relative to prior work.
weaknesses: The search space is quite narrow: a fixed-depth (L=4) fully-connected DNN where only the layer widths vary (20^4 configurations on Frappe/Diabetes). There are no skip connections, normalization choices, activation choices, or modern tabular architectures (e.g., attention-based models). Searching only over layer widths is arguably closer to hyperparameter optimization than full NAS, which weakens the significance of the search methodology and of the 'global best AUC' target.

ExpressFlow appears to be a relatively incremental modification of SynFlow: the theoretical analysis (Appendix G.3) shows neuron saliency is essentially a sum of SynFlow terms over incoming/outgoing parameters, plus layer recalibration by 1/l(z^l) and K_l. Moreover, the ablation (Table 4) shows the largest gain comes from the heuristic of forcing parameters positive (SRCC 0.51 -> 0.83 on Criteo), which is an empirical trick not well justified theoretically.

The headline 'up to 82.75x' speedup comes from the Frappe dataset; the speedup on Diabetes is only 1.75x, so the practical impact is dataset-dependent and the abstract framing overstates the uniform benefit.

Baseline coverage is limited: the anytime comparison (Figure 6) involves only two baselines (RE-NAS, TabNAS), both training-based. Stronger alternatives such as HyperBand/BOHB-style or PASHA-style progressive allocation, or surrogate-assisted methods, are not directly compared in the anytime setting on real search (they are only benchmarked on the benchmark's query interface in Section 4.1.2).

The design constants M/K ≈ 30 and U = 2 are chosen from experiments on these datasets; generalization of the budget-aware coordinator to other datasets or larger/wider search spaces is unclear. The objective in Equation 2 is heuristic rather than a principled optimization.
All three datasets are binary classification tasks with AUC as the metric; no regression or multiclass tasks are included, limiting the claimed generality of 'tabular data'.

The theoretical claims of characterizing both trainability and expressivity are loose: the derivations show connections to synaptic saliency terms, but the link from the final score (Equation 12) to expressivity/trajectory length arguments is largely intuitive rather than established.
